  REPORT TO THE CITY COUNCIL

AGENDA ITEM
Report: Plans and Specifications for the Emerald Isle 1850 Tank and Cooks Canyon
  Tank Rehabilitation Project.

  1) Resolution adopting Specification No. 4008 and Plan No. 7000-E-1 for the
  Emerald Isle 1850 Tank and Cooks Canyon Water Tank Rehabilitation
  Project, and directing the City Clerk to Advertise for Bids.

COUNCIL ACTION

 Item Type: Consent Calendar

 Approved for  July 1, 2025  calendar

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Specifications and Plans have been completed for the tank rehabilitation of Emerald
Isle 1850 Tank and Cooks Canyon Water Tank. This report requests the City Council to
adopt the project specifications and plans and authorize advertising for bids.

RECOMMENDATION
Authorize the City Manager to adopt the specification and plan for the Emerald Isle
1850 Tank and Cooks Canyon Water Tank Rehabilitation Project and direct the City
Clerk to advertise for bids.

ANALYSIS
The City of Glendale owns and operates 28 potable water reservoirs/tanks and five
recycled water tanks in the water system. During regular inspections, some tanks were
found to be in need of repairs to extend their service life and comply with current safety
standards.

In July 2016, the City hired Harper & Associates Engineering (Harper) to evaluate a
number of welded steel water storage tanks for both the potable and recycled water
systems. Harper prepared evaluation reports outlining the condition of the tank coating
systems and with recommendations to repair and/or upgrade structural and safety
deficiencies. The evaluation report also included interior and exterior photographic
surveys and laboratory analysis on the chemical components of the existing coatings.

Based on the findings and recommendations, the Water Division has implemented a
capital improvement program to systematically rehabilitate these water storage tanks.

  4b
 Emerald Isle 1850 Tank and Cooks Canyon Water Tank have been selected for the
rehabilitation in Fiscal Year 2025-2026.

The proposed work at the selected tanks includes abrasive removal of existing paint,
application of new coating systems, structural repairs, and installation of new safety
features.

To ensure competitive bids, the project will be advertised in local newspaper, the
Glendale Independent, prior to bid opening, as well as on eBidBoard, a construction
services company. In turn, eBidBoard will send the project advertisement to several
other project posting sites that do not require subscription (i.e. Bid America, Blueprint
Express, Construction Data Corp, Direct Connection, F.W. Dodge, etc.).

Specification No. 4008 and Plan No. 7000-E-1 are on file and available at the Glendale
Water & Power - Water Engineering Service Counter.

STAKEHOLDERS/OUTREACH
Not applicable.

FISCAL IMPACT
The engineer’s estimate for the construction work of this stage of the project was
$600,000 per tank, for a total of $1,200,000, which was included in the FY 2025-26
budget as outlined below. Staff will return to City Council to award a contract to the
lowest responsive bidder.

Report: Roll-up Door Replacement Project

  1. Resolution adopting Specification No. 3996 for the Roll-up Door Replacement
  Project and directing the City Clerk to advertise for bids.

COUNCIL ACTION

 Item Type: Consent Calendar

 Approved for  July 1, 2025  calendar

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
There is an immediate need to remove and replace existing roll-up doors at various Fire
Stations, as they have surpassed their useful life. The purpose of this project is to adopt
the provided specification and solicit bids for the replacement of 13 roll-up doors at Fire
Stations 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, and 29. The project involves the removal of the current
doors and the installation of new, high-performance doors that meet fire safety standards,
enhance station security, and reduce maintenance requirements.

RECOMMENDATION
Approve the Resolution adopting Specification No. 3996 for the Roll-up Door
Replacement Project and direct the City Clerk to advertise for bids.

ANALYSIS
The replacement project involves upgrading 13 roll-up doors at various fire stations to
modern direct-drive operations. These enhancements will improve functionality and
reliability across the facilities.

The existing roll-up doors have been in service for decades and have reached the end of
their operational lifespan. The new direct-drive systems will provide enhanced durability,
reduced maintenance, and improved efficiency.

Installation will be completed in phases to ensure uninterrupted station operations and
maintain safety. The project also includes the replacement or upgrade of associated
hardware, ensuring seamless integration with the stations' current infrastructure.

 STAKEHOLDERS/OUTREACH
The work will be coordinated with the contractor and Glendale Fire Department staff to
minimize disruptions to operations and the public.

FISCAL IMPACT
There is no fiscal impact associated with this report. The Roll-up Door Replacement
Project is estimated to cost $585,000, a portion of which was approved as a part of the
FY 2024-25 budget. Staff will determine if additional appropriations will be requested or
if funds can be shifted from another project at the time of contract award.

ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW (CEQA/NEPA)
This project is Categorically Exempt under the provisions of the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA) as a Class 1, Section 15301.

This item is exempt from campaign disclosure requirements.

AGENDA ITEM

Report: Amendment Seven for FY 2025-2026 Los Angeles County Aging and Disabilities
(AD) Baseline and Modernizing Older Californians Act (MOCA) Funding for Supportive
Services Program (SSP).

  1. Motion to accept $95,373 in baseline and MOCA funding from Los Angeles County
  AD for FY 2025-2026 Supportive Services Program; and authorize the City
  Manager or a designee to execute Amendment Seven to the SSP232404
  Subaward period July 2025 – July 2026 to accept and implement funding.

  2. Resolution of Appropriation to appropriate $30,273 in baseline funding for SSP
  senior case management.

COUNCIL ACTION

 Item Type: Consent Calendar

 Approved for  July 1, 2025  calendar

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Los Angeles County AD is providing grant funds in the amount of $95,373 in baseline and
MOCA funding for FY 2025-2026 to provide senior case management services through
the Community Services & Parks (CSP) Department.

Los Angeles County AD baseline and MOCA grant funding will allow the SSP to provide
case management services to seniors 60 years of age and older in the SSP program.

SSP provides annual assistance for up to 80 unduplicated seniors which includes: initial
intake, in-home assessment, care plan, information and referral services, purchase of
goods/services, annual reassessments, and well-being checkups.

RECOMMENDATION
That the City Council accept and authorize the City Manager to execute Amendment
Seven to the SSP232404 subaward period July 2025–June 2026 to accept and
implement $95,373 in baseline and MOCA funding from Los Angeles County AD for the
FY 2025-26 SSP and appropriate $30,273 in funds for senior case management services.

4d
25-88327
 ANALYSIS
CSP has been operating SSP, better known as senior case management, since 1992.
The SSP provides comprehensive, long-term services to seniors 60 years of age and
older, that utilize a case manager’s professional skills and competence to serve senior
clients and link them to a full range of appropriate services including service coordination,
care planning, purchase of goods/services, benefits enrollment, and referral services.
The primary goal is to assist the elderly in maintaining their independence and living in
their own homes. The SSP is operated through the Senior Services Unit which also
provides long-term services that include the Elderly Nutrition Program, Emergency Meals,
and Telephone Reassurance Program.

Los Angeles County AD originally awarded CSP an SSP subaward through a
noncompetitive process whereby the City enters into a subaward agreement for a one-
year term, commencing July 1, 2023, through June 30, 2024, with three additional options
to renew annually for an anticipated total subaward term of four years. Baseline funding
for the program requires a 12% cash match. Amendment Seven is part of year three of
the four-year subaward term and commences July 1, 2025, through June 30, 2026. No
cash match is required for MOCA funding.

SSP MOCA funds are allocated from the State of California to provide assistance of case
managers in the daily operations of the program including home visits, case planning,
monitoring, contract compliance, invoicing, purchase of goods/service, and data tracking
and direct assistance to seniors for case management services. Examples of direct
assistance include payment of a utility bill, home cleaning, respite, and purchase of small
appliances, clothing, medical equipment/supplies, etc.

SSP assists up to 80 unduplicated seniors sixty years of age and older each fiscal year,
with the following senior case management services: initial intake screening, in-home
assessment, service authorization, care plan, and connecting to other services. Service
areas for SSP include Glendale, La Crescenta, Montrose, and Verdugo City.

The period that MOCA funding is available for use is from July 1, 2025, through February
28, 2026.

STAKEHOLDERS/OUTREACH
The SSP is part of the Senior Services Unit which operates out of the Adult Recreation
Center. Program services are advertised quarterly in the CSP Leisure Guide, CSP
Newsletter, on the Department website and social media, and outreach is conducted with
community agencies to ensure the public is aware of the available services.

FISCAL IMPACT
Los Angeles County AD awarded the City $95,373 in SSP baseline and MOCA grant
awards from for FY 2025-26. $65,100 was appropriated as part of the FY2025-2026
budget process; thus, staff is requesting that the Council appropriate an additional
$30,273 from grant revenue to SSP baseline.

Report: 2025-2026 Insurance Renewals

Motion authorizing the annual renewal of insurance policies for the City's property, excess
liability, workers' compensation, cyber liability, and other miscellaneous coverages for
2025-26 fiscal year, in an amount not-to-exceed $9,206,520.00.

COUNCIL ACTION

 Item Type: Consent Item

 Approved for  July 1, 2025  calendar

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Staff seeks Council approval for annual renewal of liability insurance policies for excess
liability, property, workers’ compensation, cyber liability and other miscellaneous policies.

4e
25-88345
 RECOMMENDATION
That the City Council authorize the renewal of the excess insurance policies for the City’s
excess liability, property, Workers’ Compensation, cyber liability and other miscellaneous
coverages for a total “not-to-exceed” amount of $9,206,520.00.

ANALYSIS
The City is self-insured for various losses, with self-insured retention amounts ranging
from $10,000 to $2 million. The following is a brief description of the various lines of
insurance coverages the City currently has and intends to renew:

Property

Property insurance covers loss, theft, or damage to City-owned property. An example of
this type of loss includes damages caused by fire, wind, vandalism, etc. In order to secure
the most advantageous rates for this insurance, the City purchases two separate policies.
The first policy covers property owned by Glendale Water & Power because of the nature
of the property and equipment. The broker for this policy specializes in utility operations
and can obtain a lower price for this insurance. The second policy provides coverage for
all other City property.

Excess Liability

The excess liability policy provides coverage for damages for a loss as a result of an act,
or failure to act, by a City of Glendale employee. Examples of this type of loss include
automobile accidents, dangerous conditions of public property, police liability,
employment claims etc.

This year we have been offered an Individual Member Corridor Deductible (IMCD). This
is option is for members with good loss experience and offers a way to maintain a lower
premium without increasing the overall Self-Insured Retention (SIR). While the SIR
remains at $2M for each and every claim, the IMCD sits above the SIR, and erodes as
claims are paid for the policy period. For claims that go above $2M, the City covers the
cost of the claim until the $1M IMCD is spent. Once that $1M corridor is exhausted,
PRISM resumes full payment for any claim above the City’s $2M SIR. In short, the
corridor deductible is like a “buffer zone” the City takes on temporarily. Once that buffer
is used up, the regular coverage rules go back into effect and PRISM picks up anything
above the City’s $2 million SIR. Utilizing the IMCD will reduce the excess liability premium
by approximately $1 million, making it an economical yet risk-justified approach for excess
coverage.

Workers’ Compensation

This coverage pays costs for Workers’ Compensation claims that exceed the City’s SIR.

4e  2
25-88345
 Fine Arts

The fine art insurance covers losses to artwork owned by the City, as well as the periodic
art exhibitions held at the Brand Library and Art Center.

Aviation

Aviation coverage provides protection for the City's liability due to the Police Department’s
Helicopter Operations.

Crime

This policy covers losses associated with employee theft, fraudulent activity, and other
criminal acts.

Verdugo Crime Lab

This insurance covers losses from a claim in the event an error or omission is made by
an employee working at the Verdugo Crime Lab.

Cyber Liability

The cyber liability policy is designed to cover the costs associated with a compromise of
electronic data. Examples of this could include unauthorized access to sensitive data,
information released as a result of human error or equipment malfunction, intentional theft
of data, etc. Recoverable costs include the costs to retrieve lost or stolen data as well
costs associated with assessments and training to prevent future losses.

The City’s insurance brokers have been working with PRISM and other carriers to secure
the best rates for the City (a copy of the proposed rates is attached hereto). A majority of
the policy rates have remained steady (Fine Arts, Aviation, Verdugo Crime Lab). The
worker’s compensation coverage had a slight increase, but only due to an increase in
payroll, not due to claims or other factors. Finally, as expected, the excess liability policy
has the greatest increase, due in part to claims, but mostly due to market conditions. The
premium amounts listed are “not to exceed amounts” and the final cost may be less than
the maximum amount of $9,206,520.00. Funding for the insurance premiums is currently
budgeted for in the Liability, Workers’ Compensation and Department budgets. Additional
appropriation of funds is not necessary. GWP property insurance will be charged to GWP
(Electric Works Revenue and Water Works Revenue Funds), Fine Arts insurance will be
charged to Library (General Fund), and Verdugo Crime Lab will be charged to Police
(General Fund) via a journal entry. Aviation insurance will be directly charged to Police
and is budgeted for in the Joint Air Support Fund.

AGENDA ITEM

Report: Standardization of Knox Corporation Products

1. Resolution to dispense with competitive bidding to establish the Knox Corporation as
the City's standard narcotic safe manufacturer and authorizing the Deputy Director of
Finance/Purchasing to procure related software, hardware, parts, maintenance, and
services.

COUNCIL ACTION

 Item Type: Action Item

 Approved for  July 1, 2025  calendar

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The Glendale Fire Department requests approval to designate Knox Corporation (Knox)
as the exclusive vendor for secure narcotic access and storage solutions. This request is
due to the need to replace outdated narcotics safes in the emergency response fleet and
the long-term goal of standardizing equipment for security, efficiency, and interoperability.
The current safes have exceeded their service life and lack necessary security features
required for compliance with regulations. The Fire Department, in collaboration with the
IT Department, has piloted three Knox narcotic safes on multiple emergency apparatus
resources over the last year and these safes have shown reliability and ease of use, with
benefits such as reduced access time in emergencies and improved inventory tracking.
Knox is recognized for providing secure access solutions for first responders at both
regional and national levels, with a reputation for quality and durability, and have proven
to be considered the gold standard for our narcotic storage needs. The Fire Department
has used Knox products for key storage solutions over multiple decades and has always
been satisfied with their products and service and have been equally pleased with their
narcotic safe products in the past year.

RECOMMENDATION
Dispense with competitive bidding establishing Knox Corporation as the City standard
manufacturer and authorizing the Deputy Director of Finance-Purchasing to procure
related software, hardware, parts, maintenance, and services.

8a
25-88175
 ANALYSIS
The Glendale Fire Department must maintain a narcotic storage system in accordance
with State and Federal regulations. When the current narcotic storage system vendor was
sold to a new company after approximately ten years of use, our hardware was deemed
to have reached the end of life and would therefore not be supported by the new company.
In collaboration with the IT Department, Staff then researched the best replacement
solution and has determined through a pilot program that the Knox product is the gold
standard for our narcotic storage needs. Given the stringent regulations enforced by the
Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) and other regulatory authorities, it is imperative that our
equipment is reliable in both hardware and software. Our current mixed fleet of safes
presents a risk to our accountability; however, transitioning to an exclusive fleet of Knox
products would mitigate this concern. The current safes have surpassed their service life
and lack critical security features necessary for regulatory compliance. Knox safes offer
essential features such as PIN/password access, detailed audit histories, and tamper-
evident designs. These are crucial for ensuring secure and accountable handling of
controlled substances, minimizing diversion risks, and maintaining compliance.

Pilot Program: In collaboration with the IT Department, the Fire Department successfully
piloted three Knox narcotic safes on multiple emergency apparatus resources.

Evaluation: The pilot program included a comprehensive evaluation of the Knox safes'
performance. Key aspects evaluated were ease of use, reliability, security features, and
system integration.

Compliance: The compliance of Knox safes with DEA regulations and other relevant laws
was verified.

Cost-Benefit Analysis: A cost-benefit analysis compared the costs of maintaining the
current mixed fleet versus converting to an exclusive fleet of Knox products. The analysis
revealed that the long-term benefits of standardizing Knox products—including improved
security, reduced maintenance costs, and enhanced efficiency—outweigh the initial
investment.

By converting to an exclusive fleet of Knox products, the Glendale Fire Department will
enhance its ability to securely and efficiently manage controlled substances, ensure
regulatory compliance, and improve overall operational effectiveness.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

On March 26, 2024, the City Council considered two reports regarding the City’s Mayor
Selection Policy (“Policy”) set forth in Glendale Municipal Code (“GMC”) section
2.04.020 and directed staff to prepare alternatives to the Policy for the Council’s
consideration and further direction. Since then, the Council has held two mayoral
selections invoking the “best interest” provision of subsection (H) of Section 2.04.020
(“Best Interest Clause”).

As directed by the Council, staff presents alternatives to modify the Policy’s seniority
rule by providing a preference for councilmembers who have not served as mayor,
provided they have served a minimum amount of time on Council, e.g. 1 or 2 years.
Staff also provides alternatives to the provision regarding selection during the last year
of a councilmember’s term, and changes to the Best Interest Clause. One option is to
eliminate the “best interest” language and replace it with specified circumstances under
which the Council can select a councilmember other than as otherwise required by the
Policy. Another option is to retain the Best Interest Clause, but modify it to shift its
apparent focus from the councilmember purportedly being “skipped over” to the best
interest being served by selecting another councilmember. Legally, as the courts have
held, there is no difference, but such a change could remove the stigma associated with
invocation of “best interest.”

Council may also want to consider changing the mayoral selection date to sometime in
July or later after municipal elections and seating of new councilmembers. Finally, an
option is available to Council to repeal or scale back the Policy and revert back to the
process that simply gives preference for councilmembers who have served some time
on Council prior to mayor selection.

  8b
 RECOMMENDATION
Staff has no recommendation. Staff has provided alternate Code language in this Report
for Council’s consideration and direction. Alternatively, the Council may also choose to
repeal the Policy and revert to the previous process where the Council was only required
to give preference to councilmembers who had the benefit of council experience prior to
the time of selection.

ANALYSIS
Current Mayoral Selection Policy

On March 30, 2021, the Council adopted Ordinance No. 5963, amending the GMC
relating to the Policy for the annual selection of the mayor. For purposes relevant for
this Report, GMC Section 2.04.020 provides:

  Subsection (B) – Seniority Rule and Tiebreakers

  •  The councilmember with the longest continuous service since last serving as
  Mayor shall be appointed mayor unless one of the exceptions apply. (Subsection
  (B)(1)).

  •  Tiebreakers between councilmembers with the longest continuous service are
  resolved in favor of the councilmember who received the most votes in the most
  recent election or higher percentage of votes if the councilmembers were elected
  in different elections. (Subsection (B)(2)).

  Subsections (C), (D) and (G) - Limitations on Appointments

  Subsections (C), (D) and (G) address limitations on appointments.

  •  Subsection (C) generally prohibits the appointment of a councilmember whose
  term would expire in the same year as the mayoral term or whose term will expire
  within 180 days after the date of selection may not be selected mayor. This
  provision is intended to prevent a councilmember from having an advantage of
  seeking reelection to Council while having the title of mayor.

  •  Subsection (D) limits the sitting from mayor being reappointed to the subsequent
  term unless all other councilmembers decline to serve.

  •  Subsection (E) limits the appointment of a councilmember appointed to fill a
  vacancy on council to the mayorship unless there is no viable alternative.

  Subsections (E) & (F) – Appointments When Mayorship Not Accepted or When
  Mayor Vacates or Is Removed

  •  Subsection (E) provides that the councilmember in line to be appointed in
  accordance with the Policy is unwilling or unable to serve, the council is to select

  2  8b
   the next eligible councilmember in line of seniority and the councilmember who
  deferred is placed next in the seniority line.

  •  Subsection (F) provides that the councilmember serving as mayor vacates or is
  removed from his or her council seat, the Council can choose any
  councilmember to be mayor and that councilmember will not be prejudiced in
  serving a scheduled term.

  Subsection (H) – Best Interest Clause

  •  The “Best Interest Clause – Subsection (H) provides that “notwithstanding the
  provisions of this section,” the Council has the discretion to not choose the
  councilmember with the longest continuous service on the Council if it finds it is
  in the City’s “best interest” to do so and can select the next qualified
  councilmember.

Subsequent Implementation and Interpretation of Section 2.04.020

Subsequent to the March 2024 discussion of the Policy, the Council has held two
mayoral selections. In each case, the Council selected a councilmember who was not
“next in line” under Subsection B and chose another councilmember by invoking the
Best Interest Clause.

The Policy and the contours of the Best Interest Clause were also the subject of
litigation. Najarian v. City of Glendale, L.A.S.C. Case No. 24STCP02101. In the
litigation, the Court confirmed that selection of the mayor is a legislative and political act
and that invocation of the Best Interest Clause will not be overturned by a court unless
the decision is arbitrary or capricious. As a legislative act, the Court found that the city
“need not make explicit findings to support its action. A court cannot inquire into the
wisdom of a legislative act or review the merits of a local government’s policy
decisions.” (citing Federation of Hillside & Canyon Assn’s. v. City of Los Angeles (2004)
126 Cal.App.th 1180.) “Furthermore, the mental process principle “precludes any
judicially authorized inquiry into the subjective motives or mental processes of
legislators.” (citing County of Los Angeles v. Superior Court (1975) 13 Cal.3d 721, 726.)

Applying this “extremely deferential” standard of review, the Court upheld the 2024
mayoral selection and the Council’s invocation of the Best Interest Clause finding that
the councilmembers sufficiently stated reasons for making the best interest
determination without a need to make any specific findings relative to the
councilmember who was passed over.

Other Considerations

Change of the Mayoral Selection Date

As required by the GMC, the mayor is currently selected at the regular meeting
occurring after the first Monday in April. Mayor selection has historically occurred in
April although it previously occurred later in April when the City’s general municipal
elections were held in April of odd-numbered years. The City’s general municipal
elections now coincide with the dates of the statewide primary elections, which are in
March in presidential election years (2024, 2028, etc.) and June in non-presidential
election years (2026, 2030 etc.). Thus, mayor selection is occurring prior to the seating
of new councilmembers. Even after the March elections, mayor selection is occurring
before new councilmembers are sworn in due to the length of time it takes Los Angeles
County to certify election results.

  7  8b
 During a discussion of the Policy at the April 1, 2025 meeting, the Council inquired
about changing the mayor selection date. To ensure mayor selection occurs after the
City holds its municipal elections, the Council may want to consider mid-to-late July, or
later. If the Council makes a change, it would have to decide when that change would
take effect and its applicability to the current mayor’s term.

Consideration of Repeal of Policy

The Policy was adopted for the purpose of providing a level of certainty in the mayor
selection process. As noted, in the last two years, the Council has utilized the Best
Interest Clause to select a councilmember who was not next in line under the Seniority
Rule. Suffice it to say this has caused consternation from segments of the community,
especially from supporters of those councilmembers who were next in line under the
current seniority rule. Although the Council may make changes to eliminate or soften
the impact of the seniority rule, it is difficult to predict that a revised rule will in all
circumstances result in decisions that will be deemed fair. For example, by granting
preference to ensure councilmembers who have not previously served as mayor can do
so during their first term, it is possible more seasoned councilmembers could get
skipped over if new councilmembers come aboard every election cycle. One option for
consideration is to repeal the Policy and revert to the prior ordinance which simply gave
preference to councilmembers who had some experience on council prior to mayor
selection. Returning to the prior policy would permit Council to choose a mayor based
on who the Council feels is the appropriate choice for that particular year, without the
level of angst that has occurred when it is perceived a councilmember is being “skipped
over.”

Staff requests City Council direction on the above options presented, as well as on any
other provisions of the currently existing ordinance which Council would like to modify.
